What it tests: Converting a sentence from Active voice (subject performs the action) to Passive voice (subject receives the action), or vice versa.

questions.q: In the following question, there are six sentences marked S1, S6, P, Q, R, S. The positions of S1 and S6 are fixed. You are required to choose one of the four alternatives which would be the most logical sequence of the sentence in the passage. S1. For a conversation to be stimulating and sustained, the participants must be active talkers as well as active listeners. P: This is usually unnecessary, confusing and even boring to your partner. Q: Some people feel that they have to give long-winded explanations of their views. R: Make a point of throwing the conversational ball to the other person after you have presented your ideas in an abridged form. S: Be sure to do both in conversation. S6. It's better to paint the big picture first, and if your partner wants to know more, you can always fill in with details.
questions.theory:
What it tests: Rearranging jumbled sentences/parts into a logically coherent paragraph.
Trick: Find the opening sentence first — it introduces the topic and has NO pronoun referring back to something earlier (no 'he/it/this/they' referring to an unnamed noun). Then follow connector words: 'however/but' signals contrast with the previous sentence; 'therefore/thus' signals a result; 'firstly...secondly' signals sequence.
Example: A. It was raining heavily. B. The match had already started when it happened. C. So the match was postponed. → Correct order: A → C → B is wrong since B references 'it' (the rain) — correct logical order is A (sets the scene) → C (result) → B is misplaced; proper technique: A introduces rain, C gives the consequence (postponement), confirming A→C is a clean cause-effect pair to start with.

questions.q: In the sentence, identify the segment which contains the grammatical error. India export 12.01 million tonnes of rice and four million tonnes of sugar in the past five years.
questions.theory:
What it tests: Identifying which segment/part of a sentence contains a grammatical mistake.
Trick: Check these 5 things in order, in every segment: (1) Subject-Verb agreement (singular/plural match), (2) Tense consistency across the sentence, (3) Correct preposition usage, (4) Article usage (a/an/the), (5) Parallelism in lists/comparisons. Most errors in these papers fall into one of these 5 buckets.
Example: "Each of the students *have* submitted their assignment." → Error: 'have' should be 'has' (subject 'Each' is singular, even though 'of the students' looks plural).

What it tests: Rearranging jumbled sentences/parts into a logically coherent paragraph.
Trick: Find the opening sentence first — it introduces the topic and has NO pronoun referring back to something earlier (no 'he/it/this/they' referring to an unnamed noun). Then follow connector words: 'however/but' signals contrast with the previous sentence; 'therefore/thus' signals a result; 'firstly...secondly' signals sequence.
Example: A. It was raining heavily. B. The match had already started when it happened. C. questions.theory:
What it tests: Converting a sentence from Active voice (subject performs the action) to Passive voice (subject receives the action), or vice versa.
Trick (Active → Passive): Object of active sentence → becomes subject of passive. Verb → changes to 'be + past participle' (is/was/were + V3). Subject of active sentence → becomes 'by + agent' at the end (often optional). Tense of 'be' must match the original tense of the active verb.
Example: Active: "The chef cooked the meal." → Passive: "The meal was cooked by the chef."

questions.theory:
What it tests: Converting a sentence from Active voice (subject performs the action) to Passive voice (subject receives the action), or vice versa.
Trick (Active → Passive): Object of active sentence → becomes subject of passive. Verb → changes to 'be + past participle' (is/was/were + V3). Subject of active sentence → becomes 'by + agent' at the end (often optional). Tense of 'be' must match the original tense of the active verb.
Example: Active: "The chef cooked the meal." → Passive: "The meal was cooked by the chef."

questions.theory:
What it tests: Choosing the single word that is both grammatically correct and contextually appropriate for a blank in a sentence.

What it tests: Identifying which segment/part of a sentence contains a grammatical mistake.

questions.theory:
What it tests: Converting a quoted sentence (Direct Speech) into a reported sentence (Indirect Speech), or vice versa.

R: The old pattern of his life in which his parents were the nucleus around which his life revolved now undergoes a change. S: He finds himself in an emotional void which he must fill somehow. S6. questions.theory:
What it tests: Rearranging jumbled sentences/parts into a logically coherent paragraph.
Trick: Find the opening sentence first — it introduces the topic and has NO pronoun referring back to something earlier (no 'he/it/this/they' referring to an unnamed noun). Then follow connector words: 'however/but' signals contrast with the previous sentence; 'therefore/thus' signals a result; 'firstly...secondly' signals sequence.
Example: A. It was raining heavily. B. The match had already started when it happened. C. So the match was postponed. → Correct order: A → C → B is wrong since B references 'it' (the rain) — correct logical order is A (sets the scene) → C (result) → B is misplaced; proper technique: A introduces rain, C gives the consequence (postponement), confirming A→C is a clean cause-effect pair to start with.

questions.q: In the following question, a sentence has been given in Active/Passive Voice. Out of the four alternatives suggested, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in Passive/Active Voice. Dora located the building on the map.
questions.a: The building was located by Dora on the map.
questions.theory:
What it tests: Converting a sentence from Active voice (subject performs the action) to Passive voice (subject receives the action), or vice versa.
Trick (Active → Passive): Object of active sentence → becomes subject of passive. Verb → changes to 'be + past participle' (is/was/were + V3). Subject of active sentence → becomes 'by + agent' at the end (often optional). Tense of 'be' must match the original tense of the active verb.
Example: Active: "The chef cooked the meal." → Passive: "The meal was cooked by the chef."

questions.q: In the below question, a sentence has been given in Direct/Indirect speech. Out of the four alternatives suggested, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in Indirect/Direct speech. Rahul requested me to pass the salt.
questions.a: "Please pass the salt," Rahul said to me.
questions.theory:
What it tests: Converting a quoted sentence (Direct Speech) into a reported sentence (Indirect Speech), or vice versa.
Trick (Direct → Indirect): (1) Remove quotation marks, add 'that' (or whether/if for questions). (2) Shift tense one step back (Present→Past, Past→Past Perfect). (3) Change pronouns to match the reporter's perspective. (4) Shift time/place words: today→that day, tomorrow→the next day, here→there, this→that.
Example: Direct: He said, "I am happy." → Indirect: He said that he was happy. (am → was, tense shifts back one step)

questions.q: In the following question, sentence given with a blank to be filled in with an appropriate word. Four alternatives are suggested for the question. Choose the correct alternative out of the four and indicate it by selecting the appropriate option. Although his army equalled the Texan army in numbers and __________ it in equipment, he dared not force a fight.
questions.theory:
What it tests: Choosing the single word that is both grammatically correct and contextually appropriate for a blank in a sentence.
Trick: Read the whole sentence first (not just up to the blank) — the answer often depends on a word AFTER the blank. Eliminate options that are grammatically wrong first (wrong tense/part of speech), then pick the most contextually precise word among what's left — near-synonyms are often used as distractors.
Example: "He was _____ tired to walk any further." → 'too' (not 'so', because 'too...to' is the fixed grammatical pattern here).

questions.theory:
What it tests: A bracketed part of a sentence may need to be replaced with better/correct wording; pick the best option, which may be 'No improvement needed'.
Trick: First judge if the bracketed part is already grammatically correct AND natural-sounding — if yes, the answer is usually 'No substitution/improvement required', a genuine trap many students avoid by force-picking a change. Otherwise, look for the same 5 error types as Sentence Error Spotting above.
Example: "She is one of the student (who has) passed." → Improve to: "who have" (relative clause after 'one of the students who...' takes a plural verb).

questions.q: In the following question, one part of the sentence may have an error. Identify the segment which contains the grammatical error and select the appropriate option. Digestive problems have been increasingly linked to the infections, but research is mixed on where common a symptom it is.
questions.theory:
What it tests: Identifying which segment/part of a sentence contains a grammatical mistake.
Trick: Check these 5 things in order, in every segment: (1) Subject-Verb agreement (singular/plural match), (2) Tense consistency across the sentence, (3) Correct preposition usage, (4) Article usage (a/an/the), (5) Parallelism in lists/comparisons. Most errors in these papers fall into one of these 5 buckets.
Example: "Each of the students *have* submitted their assignment." → Error: 'have' should be 'has' (subject 'Each' is singular, even though 'of the students' looks plural).

P: In the still theoretical structure, an attempt is being made to create a house that is "a domestication of an ecosystem". Q: What is happening in the architecture is a shift from the international style of the postindustrial era to a symbolic structure. R: Since architecture is the collective unconscious made visible, the architect does not himself always understand the full cultural implications of his own work. S: The new form is not a celebration of power over new materials, but a celebration of cooperation with ecosystem. S6. questions.theory:
What it tests: Rearranging jumbled sentences/parts into a logically coherent paragraph.
Trick: Find the opening sentence first — it introduces the topic and has NO pronoun referring back to something earlier (no 'he/it/this/they' referring to an unnamed noun). Then follow connector words: 'however/but' signals contrast with the previous sentence; 'therefore/thus' signals a result; 'firstly...secondly' signals sequence.
Example: A. It was raining heavily. B. The match had already started when it happened. C. So the match was postponed. → Correct order: A → C → B is wrong since B references 'it' (the rain) — correct logical order is A (sets the scene) → C (result) → B is misplaced; proper technique: A introduces rain, C gives the consequence (postponement), confirming A→C is a clean cause-effect pair to start with.

questions.q: In the following question, a sentence has been given in Active/Passive Voice. Out of the four alternatives suggested, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in Passive/Active Voice. Tom found the money.
questions.a: The money was found by Tom.
questions.theory:
What it tests: Converting a sentence from Active voice (subject performs the action) to Passive voice (subject receives the action), or vice versa.
Trick (Active → Passive): Object of active sentence → becomes subject of passive. Verb → changes to 'be + past participle' (is/was/were + V3). Subject of active sentence → becomes 'by + agent' at the end (often optional). Tense of 'be' must match the original tense of the active verb.
Example: Active: "The chef cooked the meal." → Passive: "The meal was cooked by the chef."

questions.theory:
What it tests: Choosing the single word that is both grammatically correct and contextually appropriate for a blank in a sentence.

questions.q: Select the segment which has an error. Camels have long, shaggy coats to keeps warm in the summer.

What it tests: Identifying which segment/part of a sentence contains a grammatical mistake.
Trick: Check these 5 things in order, in every segment: (1) Subject-Verb agreement (singular/plural match), (2) Tense consistency across the sentence, (3) Correct preposition usage, (4) Article usage (a/an/the), (5) Parallelism in lists/comparisons. Most errors in these papers fall into one of these 5 buckets.
Example: "Each of the students *have* submitted their assignment." → Error: 'have' should be 'has' (subject 'Each' is singular, even though 'of the students' looks plural).

questions.theory:
What it tests: Converting a quoted sentence (Direct Speech) into a reported sentence (Indirect Speech), or vice versa.
Trick (Direct → Indirect): (1) Remove quotation marks, add 'that' (or whether/if for questions). (2) Shift tense one step back (Present→Past, Past→Past Perfect). (3) Change pronouns to match the reporter's perspective. (4) Shift time/place words: today→that day, tomorrow→the next day, here→there, this→that.
Example: Direct: He said, "I am happy." → Indirect: He said that he was happy. (am → was, tense shifts back one step)

questions.theory:
What it tests: Converting a sentence from Active voice (subject performs the action) to Passive voice (subject receives the action), or vice versa.

questions.theory:
What it tests: Identifying which segment/part of a sentence contains a grammatical mistake.
Trick: Check these 5 things in order, in every segment: (1) Subject-Verb agreement (singular/plural match), (2) Tense consistency across the sentence, (3) Correct preposition usage, (4) Article usage (a/an/the), (5) Parallelism in lists/comparisons. questions.theory:
What it tests: Converting a sentence from Active voice (subject performs the action) to Passive voice (subject receives the action), or vice versa.
Trick (Active → Passive): Object of active sentence → becomes subject of passive. Verb → changes to 'be + past participle' (is/was/were + V3). Subject of active sentence → becomes 'by + agent' at the end (often optional). Tense of 'be' must match the original tense of the active verb.
Example: Active: "The chef cooked the meal." → Passive: "The meal was cooked by the chef."

questions.theory:
What it tests: Rearranging jumbled sentences/parts into a logically coherent paragraph.
Trick: Find the opening sentence first — it introduces the topic and has NO pronoun referring back to something earlier (no 'he/it/this/they' referring to an unnamed noun). Then follow connector words: 'however/but' signals contrast with the previous sentence; 'therefore/thus' signals a result; 'firstly...secondly' signals sequence.
Example: A. It was raining heavily. B. The match had already started when it happened. C. questions.q: In the following question, a sentence has been given in Direct/Indirect Speech. Out of the four alternatives suggested, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in Indirect/Direct Speech and select your answer. The master said to his servant, “If you don’t work efficiently, I will dismiss you.”
questions.a: The master told his servant that if he did not work efficiently, he would dismiss him.
questions.theory:
What it tests: Converting a quoted sentence (Direct Speech) into a reported sentence (Indirect Speech), or vice versa.
Trick (Direct → Indirect): (1) Remove quotation marks, add 'that' (or whether/if for questions). (2) Shift tense one step back (Present→Past, Past→Past Perfect). (3) Change pronouns to match the reporter's perspective. (4) Shift time/place words: today→that day, tomorrow→the next day, here→there, this→that.
Example: Direct: He said, "I am happy." → Indirect: He said that he was happy. (am → was, tense shifts back one step)

questions.theory:
What it tests: Converting a sentence from Active voice (subject performs the action) to Passive voice (subject receives the action), or vice versa.
Trick (Active → Passive): Object of active sentence → becomes subject of passive. Verb → changes to 'be + past participle' (is/was/were + V3). Subject of active sentence → becomes 'by + agent' at the end (often optional). Tense of 'be' must match the original tense of the active verb.
Example: Active: "The chef cooked the meal." → Passive: "The meal was cooked by the chef."

What it tests: Identifying which segment/part of a sentence contains a grammatical mistake.

questions.theory:
What it tests: Converting a sentence from Active voice (subject performs the action) to Passive voice (subject receives the action), or vice versa.

Example: Active: "The chef cooked the meal." → Passive: "The meal was cooked by the chef."

questions.q: In the following question a sentence is given in Direct/Indirect speech. Out of the four alternatives choose the one which best expresses the same sentence in Indirect/Direct Speech. Raveena said to Biyanka, “We have some more issues to deal with.”
questions.a: Raveena told Biyanka that they had some more issues to deal with.
questions.theory:
What it tests: Converting a quoted sentence (Direct Speech) into a reported sentence (Indirect Speech), or vice versa.
Trick (Direct → Indirect): (1) Remove quotation marks, add 'that' (or whether/if for questions). (2) Shift tense one step back (Present→Past, Past→Past Perfect). (3) Change pronouns to match the reporter's perspective. (4) Shift time/place words: today→that day, tomorrow→the next day, here→there, this→that.
Example: Direct: He said, "I am happy." → Indirect: He said that he was happy. (am → was, tense shifts back one step)

questions.q: In the following question, some parts of the sentence may have errors. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and select the appropriate option. If a sentence is free from error, select No Error. The more tension he takes, more his blood pressure rises.
questions.theory:
What it tests: Identifying which segment/part of a sentence contains a grammatical mistake.
Trick: Check these 5 things in order, in every segment: (1) Subject-Verb agreement (singular/plural match), (2) Tense consistency across the sentence, (3) Correct preposition usage, (4) Article usage (a/an/the), (5) Parallelism in lists/comparisons. Most errors in these papers fall into one of these 5 buckets.
Example: "Each of the students *have* submitted their assignment." → Error: 'have' should be 'has' (subject 'Each' is singular, even though 'of the students' looks plural).

Then follow connector words: 'however/but' signals contrast with the previous sentence; 'therefore/thus' signals a result; 'firstly...secondly' signals sequence.

Celebrated as the anniversary of the birth of lord Jesus, it is also a worldwide cultural and commercial phenomenon. R. Christmas is celebrated on December 25 and is a sacred religious holiday.
questions.theory:
What it tests: Rearranging jumbled sentences/parts into a logically coherent paragraph.
Trick: Find the opening sentence first — it introduces the topic and has NO pronoun referring back to something earlier (no 'he/it/this/they' referring to an unnamed noun). Then follow connector words: 'however/but' signals contrast with the previous sentence; 'therefore/thus' signals a result; 'firstly...secondly' signals sequence.
Example: A. It was raining heavily. B. The match had already started when it happened. C. So the match was postponed. → Correct order: A → C → B is wrong since B references 'it' (the rain) — correct logical order is A (sets the scene) → C (result) → B is misplaced; proper technique: A introduces rain, C gives the consequence (postponement), confirming A→C is a clean cause-effect pair to start with.

What it tests: Choosing the single word that is both grammatically correct and contextually appropriate for a blank in a sentence.
Trick: Read the whole sentence first (not just up to the blank) — the answer often depends on a word AFTER the blank. Eliminate options that are grammatically wrong first (wrong tense/part of speech), then pick the most contextually precise word among what's left — near-synonyms are often used as distractors.
Example: "He was _____ tired to walk any further." → 'too' (not 'so', because 'too...to' is the fixed grammatical pattern here).

questions.q: In the following question, a sentence has been given in Active/Passive voice. Out of four alternatives suggested, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in Passive/Active voice. The squirrel was hit by the bicycle.
questions.theory:
What it tests: Converting a sentence from Active voice (subject performs the action) to Passive voice (subject receives the action), or vice versa.
Trick (Active → Passive): Object of active sentence → becomes subject of passive. Verb → changes to 'be + past participle' (is/was/were + V3). Subject of active sentence → becomes 'by + agent' at the end (often optional). Tense of 'be' must match the original tense of the active verb.
Example: Active: "The chef cooked the meal." → Passive: "The meal was cooked by the chef."

questions.q: The question below consists of a set of labelled sentences. Out of the four options given, select the most logical order of the sentences to form a coherent paragraph. P. This is despite the fact that there is a rampant migration of rural families to urban centres. Q. Generally the gains of being a unit of the urban population are less than the disadvantages and risks that are inbuilt in the urban life. R. Rural population still dominates the urban population as far as the number is considered. S. India is a country of villages.
questions.theory:
What it tests: Rearranging jumbled sentences/parts into a logically coherent paragraph.
Trick: Find the opening sentence first — it introduces the topic and has NO pronoun referring back to something earlier (no 'he/it/this/they' referring to an unnamed noun). Then follow connector words: 'however/but' signals contrast with the previous sentence; 'therefore/thus' signals a result; 'firstly...secondly' signals sequence.
Example: A. It was raining heavily. B. The match had already started when it happened. C. So the match was postponed. → Correct order: A → C → B is wrong since B references 'it' (the rain) — correct logical order is A (sets the scene) → C (result) → B is misplaced; proper technique: A introduces rain, C gives the consequence (postponement), confirming A→C is a clean cause-effect pair to start with.

questions.q: In the following question, one part of the sentence may have an error. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and select the appropriate option. We are hoping for the stronger, fastest coronal mass ejection the sun can produce.
questions.theory:
What it tests: Identifying which segment/part of a sentence contains a grammatical mistake.
Trick: Check these 5 things in order, in every segment: (1) Subject-Verb agreement (singular/plural match), (2) Tense consistency across the sentence, (3) Correct preposition usage, (4) Article usage (a/an/the), (5) Parallelism in lists/comparisons. Most errors in these papers fall into one of these 5 buckets.
Example: "Each of the students *have* submitted their assignment." → Error: 'have' should be 'has' (subject 'Each' is singular, even though 'of the students' looks plural).

questions.q: In the following question, choose the word opposite in meaning to the given word. Ubiquitous
questions.theory:
What it tests: Selecting the word most opposite in meaning to a given word.
Trick: Learn words in opposite PAIRS from the start (not in isolation) — e.g. Benevolent↔Malevolent, Verbose↔Laconic — pairs stick in memory far better than single words.
Example: "Boost" → Antonym: Decline.

questions.q: In the below question, a sentence has been given in Direct/Indirect speech. Out of the four alternatives suggested, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in Indirect/Direct speech. "Oh, that's a wonderful idea," said the boy, gratefully.
questions.a: The boy gratefully said that that was a wonderful idea.
questions.theory:
What it tests: Converting a quoted sentence (Direct Speech) into a reported sentence (Indirect Speech), or vice versa.
Trick (Direct → Indirect): (1) Remove quotation marks, add 'that' (or whether/if for questions). (2) Shift tense one step back (Present→Past, Past→Past Perfect). (3) Change pronouns to match the reporter's perspective. (4) Shift time/place words: today→that day, tomorrow→the next day, here→there, this→that.
Example: Direct: He said, "I am happy." → Indirect: He said that he was happy. (am → was, tense shifts back one step)

questions.q: In the below question, a sentence is given with one part bracketed. Select the option that provides the correct replacement for the bracketed part. In case of no improvement needed, choose 'No Improvement' option. He had been (sold into) slavery, and was still working among a gang of labourers on a farm in Gaul.
questions.theory:
What it tests: A bracketed part of a sentence may need to be replaced with better/correct wording; pick the best option, which may be 'No improvement needed'.
Trick: First judge if the bracketed part is already grammatically correct AND natural-sounding — if yes, the answer is usually 'No substitution/improvement required', a genuine trap many students avoid by force-picking a change. Otherwise, look for the same 5 error types as Sentence Error Spotting above.
Example: "She is one of the student (who has) passed." → Improve to: "who have" (relative clause after 'one of the students who...' takes a plural verb).
